name: Missing Consideration
consequence: A contract without consideration is void ab initio under common law. Under Indian Contract Act 1872, an agreement without consideration is void subject to exceptions in s.25.
recommended_action: Advise client to establish adequate consideration or restructure the agreement as a deed. In India, check if s.25 exception applies (natural love and affection, past services, time-barred debt).
legal_reference: Currie v Misa [1875] LR 10 Ex 153; Indian Contract Act 1872 s.25

name: Lack of Capacity — Minor
consequence: Contracts with a minor are void ab initio under Indian law (Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose). Under UK law they are voidable at the minor's election, except for necessaries.
recommended_action: Verify age of contracting parties. In India, contract with minor is void and cannot be ratified on majority. Obtain parental/guardian ratification under English law.
legal_reference: Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose [1903] ILR 30 Cal 539; Minors' Contracts Act 1987 (UK); Indian Contract Act 1872 s.11

name: Misrepresentation
consequence: A contract induced by misrepresentation is voidable. Fraudulent misrepresentation (Derry v Peek) entitles rescission and tort damages. Under ICA 1872 s.17-18, fraud and misrepresentation make the contract voidable.
recommended_action: Gather evidence of false statement and inducement. Consider rescission and/or damages. In India, file under s.17 (fraud) or s.18 (misrepresentation) of ICA 1872.
legal_reference: Misrepresentation Act 1967 s.2(1); Derry v Peek [1889] 14 App Cas 337; Indian Contract Act 1872 ss.17-19

name: Restraint of Trade / Non-Compete
consequence: Restraint of trade clauses are prima facie void unless reasonable. Under Indian Contract Act s.27, every agreement in restraint of trade is void subject to limited exceptions (sale of business goodwill).
recommended_action: In India — s.27 ICA renders most non-competes void; only sale of goodwill exception applies. In UK — assess geographic scope, duration, and legitimate business interest.
legal_reference: Indian Contract Act 1872 s.27; Nordenfelt v Maxim Nordenfelt [1894] AC 535; Gujarat Bottling Co v Coca Cola [1995] SC

name: Anticipatory Breach
consequence: An anticipatory breach arises when a party clearly indicates before performance is due that it will not perform. The innocent party may accept the repudiation immediately and sue, or wait until the performance date.
recommended_action: Advise the innocent party to elect promptly whether to accept or affirm; document the repudiation in writing; mitigate losses immediately upon acceptance.
legal_reference: Hochster v De La Tour [1853] 2 E&B 678; Indian Contract Act 1872 s.39

name: Exclusion and Limitation Clauses
consequence: Exclusion clauses must be incorporated, pass the contra proferentem rule, and satisfy reasonableness under UCTA 1977. Clauses excluding liability for death/personal injury from negligence are void.
recommended_action: Review incorporation (notice/signature); apply UCTA reasonableness test; advise that death/personal injury exclusions are always void. In India check ICA s.23 public policy.
legal_reference: Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 ss.2-3; Consumer Rights Act 2015 ss.62-65; Photo Production v Securicor [1980] AC 827

name: Penalty Clauses vs Liquidated Damages
consequence: A clause is enforceable as liquidated damages if it is a genuine pre-estimate of loss at the time of contracting. It is an unenforceable penalty if out of all proportion to the legitimate interest.
recommended_action: Assess whether the clause represents a genuine pre-estimate; document the commercial justification at drafting stage; consider whether Cavendish test of legitimate interest is satisfied.
legal_reference: Cavendish Square v Makdessi [2015] UKSC 67; Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre v New Garage [1915] AC 79

name: Entire Agreement Clause
consequence: An entire agreement clause excludes pre-contractual representations and oral collateral warranties. It does not prevent claims for misrepresentation or fraud but narrows the scope of collateral agreements.
recommended_action: Advise that misrepresentation claims survive entire agreement clauses; check if clause also excludes misrepresentation liability (requires specific wording subject to UCTA reasonableness).
legal_reference: Inntrepreneur Pub Co v East Crown [2000] 2 Lloyd's Rep 611; MAN Nutzfahrzeuge v Freightliner [2005] EWHC 2347

name: Frustration of Contract
consequence: Frustration discharges both parties from future obligations where a supervening event makes performance radically different from what was contracted for. Money already paid is recoverable under Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943.
recommended_action: Assess whether frustration is established; advise on money recovery under LRFCA 1943; check force majeure clause first as it may supersede frustration doctrine.
legal_reference: Davis Contractors v Fareham UDC [1956] AC 696; Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943; Indian Contract Act 1872 s.56

name: Privity of Contract
consequence: Only parties to a contract can sue on it (privity rule). Under the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999, a third party named or identified in the contract may enforce a term for their benefit.
recommended_action: Check if the contract expressly confers third-party rights; consider whether the Dunlop exception or collateral contract applies; in India privity is strictly applied under ICA.
legal_reference: Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999; Tweddle v Atkinson [1861]; Dunlop v Selfridge [1915] AC 847

name: Duress and Economic Duress
consequence: A contract entered under duress is voidable. Economic duress requires illegitimate pressure that caused the contract, with no practical alternative for the victim. Under ICA s.15, coercion makes a contract voidable.
recommended_action: Document the pressure applied and its illegitimacy; establish causation; act promptly to avoid affirmation; consider claims of unjust enrichment.
legal_reference: Universe Tankships v ITWF [1983] 1 AC 366; Atlas Express v Kafco [1989]; Indian Contract Act 1872 s.15-16

name: NDA Breach — Notification Obligation
consequence: Breach of an NDA triggers an immediate obligation to notify legal counsel and assess injunctive relief within 48 hours.
recommended_action: Notify legal counsel immediately; preserve evidence; apply for emergency injunction within 48 hours if disclosure is ongoing.
legal_reference: Coco v AN Clark (Engineers) Ltd [1969] RPC 41

name: Residual Knowledge Clause
consequence: A residuals clause may permit a recipient to use information retained in unaided memory, limiting injunctive relief.
recommended_action: Review the NDA for residuals carve-outs; advise client on scope of protection available.
legal_reference: Standard industry practice — see major cloud provider NDA templates

name: Duty of Care — Negligence
consequence: A duty of care arises where harm to the claimant was reasonably foreseeable, there is proximity, and it is fair and reasonable to impose a duty (Caparo three-stage test).
recommended_action: Establish the three-part Caparo test; obtain expert evidence on the standard of care applicable to the defendant.
legal_reference: Caparo Industries plc v Dickman [1990] 2 AC 605; Donoghue v Stevenson [1932] AC 562

name: Occupiers' Liability
consequence: An occupier owes a common duty of care to lawful visitors and a lower duty of humanity to trespassers.
recommended_action: Classify the claimant's status (visitor vs trespasser); review warning signs and maintenance records.
legal_reference: Occupiers' Liability Act 1957; Occupiers' Liability Act 1984

name: Defamation — Publication Requirement
consequence: Defamation requires a false statement of fact, published to a third party, identifying the claimant, causing serious harm. In India, defamation under IPC s.499-500 may be both civil and criminal.
recommended_action: Assess seriousness threshold; consider defences of truth, honest opinion, public interest (UK) or exceptions under IPC s.499 (India); assess criminal exposure.
legal_reference: Defamation Act 2013 s.1; Indian Penal Code ss.499-500; Sim v Stretch [1936] 2 All ER 1237

name: Product Liability
consequence: A producer is strictly liable for damage caused by a defect in their product. The claimant need not prove negligence, only the defect, damage, and causation.
recommended_action: Identify the producer in the supply chain; assess the defect type (design, manufacturing, or warning); gather product samples and technical specifications.
legal_reference: Consumer Protection Act 1987 (UK); EC Directive 85/374; Consumer Protection Act 1986 (India)

name: Vicarious Liability
consequence: An employer is vicariously liable for torts committed by an employee in the course of employment. The close connection test is used for intentional wrongs.
recommended_action: Establish employment relationship and course-of-employment; consider non-delegable duties; assess whether an independent contractor relationship breaks the chain.
legal_reference: Lister v Hesley Hall [2001] UKHL 22; Cox v Ministry of Justice [2016] UKSC 10

name: Private Nuisance
consequence: Private nuisance is an unreasonable interference with the claimant's use or enjoyment of land. Only those with a proprietary interest in the affected land can sue.
recommended_action: Advise claimant to document interference; send letter before action; seek injunction if ongoing; only landowners/tenants can bring the claim (Hunter v Canary Wharf).
legal_reference: Hunter v Canary Wharf Ltd [1997] AC 655; Cambridge Water Co v Eastern Counties Leather [1994] 2 AC 264

name: Rylands v Fletcher — Strict Liability
consequence: Strict liability arises where a person brings onto land something likely to do mischief if it escapes, the use is non-natural, and damage results from escape.
recommended_action: Assess non-natural use, foreseeability of damage, and whether the escape was caused by an act of a stranger or the claimant; consider whether Cambridge Water limits recovery.
legal_reference: Rylands v Fletcher [1868] LR 3 HL 330; Cambridge Water Co v Eastern Counties Leather [1994] 2 AC 264

name: Contributory Negligence
consequence: Where the claimant contributed to their own damage through their own negligence, damages are reduced by the proportion of their responsibility.
recommended_action: Advise defendant to raise contributory negligence; gather evidence of claimant's failure to take reasonable care; calculate proportionate apportionment.
legal_reference: Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945; Froom v Butcher [1976] QB 286

name: Economic Torts — Inducing Breach of Contract
consequence: A defendant who intentionally induces a third party to breach a contract with the claimant commits the tort of inducing breach of contract, requiring knowledge of the contract and intention to interfere.
recommended_action: Establish defendant's knowledge of the contract; prove intentional inducement; seek injunctive relief and economic loss damages.
legal_reference: OBG Ltd v Allan [2007] UKHL 21; Lumley v Gye [1853] 2 El & Bl 216

name: Psychiatric Injury — Secondary Victims
consequence: A secondary victim claiming psychiatric injury must satisfy the Alcock control mechanisms: close tie of love and affection, proximity in time and space, and perception through own unaided senses.
recommended_action: Classify claimant as primary or secondary victim; for secondary victims apply all Alcock criteria; obtain psychiatric expert evidence.
legal_reference: Alcock v Chief Constable of South Yorkshire [1992] 1 AC 310; Page v Smith [1996] AC 155

name: Copyright Infringement
consequence: Copyright infringement occurs when a substantial part of a protected work is reproduced without licence or statutory exemption. In India, Copyright Act 1957 governs; fair dealing exceptions are narrower than fair use.
recommended_action: Conduct substantial part analysis; check fair dealing / fair use defence; issue takedown notice; consider criminal complaint under Copyright Act 1957 s.63 (India).
legal_reference: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 s.16; Copyright Act 1957 (India); 17 U.S.C. §107

name: Trade Mark Infringement
consequence: Trade mark infringement requires use of an identical or similar sign for identical or similar goods/services causing likelihood of confusion. In India, the Trade Marks Act 1999 governs.
recommended_action: Run clearance search; assess likelihood of confusion; send cease-and-desist; consider opposition or cancellation proceedings at IPAB/High Court.
legal_reference: Trade Marks Act 1994 s.10 (UK); Trade Marks Act 1999 (India); EU TM Regulation 2017/1001 Art. 9

name: Patent Claim Scope and Infringement
consequence: Patent infringement is assessed against each claim element. In India, Patents Act 1970 governs. Absence of novelty or inventive step can invalidate a patent. Product patents were extended to pharmaceuticals in 2005.
recommended_action: Obtain claim chart; commission freedom-to-operate opinion; consider invalidity challenge; check s.3(d) Patents Act 1970 (India) for pharmaceutical patents.
legal_reference: Patents Act 1977 s.60 (UK); Patents Act 1970 (India) ss.48-64; 35 U.S.C. §271

name: Trade Secret and Confidential Information
consequence: Confidential information is protected in equity. The springboard doctrine prevents a defendant from retaining a head start gained by misuse even after information becomes public.
recommended_action: Issue injunction promptly; consider springboard relief; quantify head-start period; gather evidence of misappropriation.
legal_reference: Saltman Engineering v Campbell Engineering [1963] 3 All ER 413; Trade Secrets (Enforcement, etc) Regulations 2018

name: Moral Rights — Waiver
consequence: Authors of copyright works have moral rights (paternity and integrity). These can be waived in writing but not assigned. In India, moral rights under s.57 of the Copyright Act 1957 cannot be waived.
recommended_action: In UK — obtain written waiver of moral rights in commissioning agreements. In India — note that moral rights are inalienable under s.57.
legal_reference: CDPA 1988 ss.77-89; Copyright Act 1957 s.57 (India)

name: Unfair Dismissal
consequence: An employee with qualifying service may claim unfair dismissal. In UK (2 years service); in India, Industrial Disputes Act 1947 applies — 240 days service triggers retrenchment compensation.
recommended_action: Verify qualifying service; review dismissal reason; check ACAS Code / Standing Orders compliance; advise on ET1 / Labour Court time limits.
legal_reference: Employment Rights Act 1996 s.98 (UK); Industrial Disputes Act 1947 s.25F (India)

name: Discrimination — Protected Characteristic
consequence: Direct or indirect discrimination on a protected characteristic is unlawful. In India, Constitutional Arts. 15-16 prohibit discrimination. SC/ST Act and PWD Act provide additional protections.
recommended_action: Identify protected characteristic; gather comparator evidence; advise on ACAS Early Conciliation (UK) or appropriate forum (India: Labour Court, High Court, NHRC).
legal_reference: Equality Act 2010 (UK); Constitution of India Arts.15-16; Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989

name: Notice Period — Wrongful Dismissal
consequence: Wrongful dismissal is a common law breach of contract claim for failure to give proper notice. Damages are limited to the notice period. Summary dismissal without PILON clause entitles damages.
recommended_action: Calculate correct notice entitlement; check for PILON clause; advise on court or Employment Tribunal claim; consider mitigation obligations.
legal_reference: Employment Rights Act 1996 s.86; Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act 1946 (India)

name: Minimum Wage Compliance
consequence: Failure to pay the National Minimum Wage is a criminal offence and attracts HMRC enforcement with 200% penalty on arrears. In India, Minimum Wages Act 1948 sets state-specific rates.
recommended_action: Calculate arrears; notify HMRC (UK) or Labour Commissioner (India); criminal prosecution is possible for wilful non-compliance.
legal_reference: National Minimum Wage Act 1998 (UK); Minimum Wages Act 1948 (India)

name: Whistleblower Protection
consequence: A qualifying disclosure made in the public interest is protected. The employer must not subject the worker to detriment or dismissal for making a protected disclosure. Unlimited compensation available.
recommended_action: Verify the disclosure is a qualifying disclosure; ensure it was made to a prescribed person or employer; document any detriment suffered; no qualifying period for claim.
legal_reference: Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 (UK); Whistle Blowers Protection Act 2014 (India)

name: Working Time — Excessive Hours
consequence: Workers cannot be required to work more than 48 hours per week averaged over 17 weeks without an individual opt-out. Daily rest, weekly rest, and in-work rest breaks are mandatory.
recommended_action: Check opt-out agreement; calculate reference period average; ensure rest period compliance; advise on unlimited compensatory rest award.
legal_reference: Working Time Regulations 1998; EC Directive 2003/88; Factories Act 1948 (India)

name: TUPE — Transfer of Undertaking
consequence: TUPE transfers employees to the new employer on their existing terms and conditions. Dismissal connected to the transfer is automatically unfair. Existing liabilities transfer to the new employer.
recommended_action: Identify affected employees; conduct due diligence on inherited liabilities; inform and consult employees; ensure no prohibited harmonisation of terms.
legal_reference: Transfer of Undertakings (Protection of Employment) Regulations 2006; Council Directive 2001/23/EC

name: Adverse Possession
consequence: A squatter may acquire title after 12 years (unregistered land) or 10 years (registered land under LRA 2002). In India, Limitation Act 1963 Schedule Art.65 — 12 years adverse possession.
recommended_action: Check Land Registry title; serve counter-notice if LRA application received; assess interruption of possession; in India verify 12-year continuous peaceful possession.
legal_reference: Land Registration Act 2002 Sch. 6; Limitation Act 1980 s.15 (UK); Limitation Act 1963 Art.65 (India)

name: Easement — Prescription and Express Grant
consequence: A prescriptive easement may be established by 20 years of continuous, open, non-contentious use as of right. Express easements require proper formality (deed) and registration.
recommended_action: Document historic user evidence; investigate title deeds for express grants; register any easements; send obstruction notice if right of way is blocked.
legal_reference: Prescription Act 1832; Law of Property Act 1925 s.62; Wheeldon v Burrows [1879]

name: Landlord and Tenant — Repair Obligations
consequence: A landlord of a residential property let for less than 7 years is obliged to keep the structure and exterior in repair and maintain installations for water, gas, electricity, and heating.
recommended_action: Serve written notice of disrepair; if no response within reasonable time, advise on specific performance, damages, or rent withholding; refer to Environmental Health.
legal_reference: Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 s.11; Homes (Fitness for Human Habitation) Act 2018; Transfer of Property Act 1882 (India)

name: Forfeiture of Lease
consequence: Before forfeiture for breach of covenant (other than non-payment of rent), a landlord must serve a s.146 LPA 1925 notice specifying the breach, requiring remedy, and offering compensation if remediable.
recommended_action: Serve s.146 notice; allow reasonable time to remedy; advise tenant to apply promptly for relief from forfeiture in court; peaceable re-entry without court order may be unlawful for residential premises.
legal_reference: Law of Property Act 1925 s.146; Billson v Residential Apartments [1992] 1 AC 494

name: Beneficial Interest — Resulting and Constructive Trust
consequence: A beneficial interest in property may arise by resulting trust (where purchase money was contributed) or constructive trust (where there is a common intention and detrimental reliance).
recommended_action: Gather evidence of financial contributions and common intention; advise on TOLATA 1996 application for sale or occupation; register restriction at Land Registry.
legal_reference: Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996; Stack v Dowden [2007] UKHL 17; Jones v Kernott [2011] UKSC 53

name: Murder — Elements
consequence: Murder requires an unlawful killing of a human being under the King's peace with malice aforethought (intent to kill or cause grievous bodily harm). Life imprisonment is mandatory in UK. In India, IPC s.300 defines murder with s.302 prescribing death or life imprisonment.
recommended_action: Establish the mens rea (intent); consider partial defences of loss of control or diminished responsibility reducing to manslaughter; assess causation chain.
legal_reference: Homicide Act 1957 (UK); Indian Penal Code ss.299-302; R v Vickers [1957] 2 QB 664

name: Manslaughter — Gross Negligence
consequence: Gross negligence manslaughter requires a duty of care, breach of that duty, and the breach was so grossly negligent as to justify criminal liability. In India, culpable homicide not amounting to murder is under IPC s.304.
recommended_action: Commission medical/expert evidence on the standard of care; assess risk of death from defendant's conduct; consider corporate manslaughter under Corporate Manslaughter Act 2007.
legal_reference: R v Adomako [1995] 1 AC 171; Corporate Manslaughter and Corporate Homicide Act 2007; IPC s.304-A

name: Theft — Elements
consequence: Theft requires dishonest appropriation of property belonging to another with intention to permanently deprive. In India, IPC s.378 defines theft with IPC s.379 prescribing 3 years imprisonment.
recommended_action: Establish all five elements; check the Ghosh/Ivey dishonesty test; consider defences of ownership belief or lack of intent to permanently deprive.
legal_reference: Theft Act 1968 ss.1-6 (UK); Indian Penal Code ss.378-382; R v Ivey [2017] UKSC 67

name: Fraud — Fraud by False Representation
consequence: Fraud by false representation requires a false representation that the defendant knew was or might be untrue, made dishonestly with intent to gain or cause loss. IPC s.420 (cheating) and s.415 cover fraud in India.
recommended_action: Gather documentary evidence of the false representation; establish dishonesty under the Ivey test; report to Action Fraud (UK) or file FIR for IPC s.420 (India).
legal_reference: Fraud Act 2006 s.2 (UK); Indian Penal Code ss.415-420; R v Ghosh [1982] QB 1053

name: Assault and Battery — GBH / ABH
consequence: GBH s.18 (intent) carries life imprisonment. GBH s.20 (recklessness) carries 5 years. ABH s.47 requires injury beyond transient/trifling. In India, IPC ss.319-326 cover hurt and grievous hurt.
recommended_action: Establish level of injury and mens rea; commission medical evidence; in India assess whether hurt (IPC s.323) or grievous hurt (IPC s.325) applies.
legal_reference: Offences Against the Person Act 1861 ss.18, 20, 47 (UK); Indian Penal Code ss.319-326

name: Self-Defence
consequence: A person may use reasonable and proportionate force in self-defence. In India, IPC ss.96-106 provide the right of private defence of person and property; there is no duty to retreat.
recommended_action: Assess whether the defendant honestly believed force was necessary; evaluate proportionality; in India check whether the right of private defence was exceeded.
legal_reference: Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008 s.76 (UK); Indian Penal Code ss.96-106

name: Diminished Responsibility
consequence: Diminished responsibility reduces murder to manslaughter where the defendant suffers an abnormality of mental functioning arising from a recognised medical condition that substantially impaired responsibility.
recommended_action: Commission forensic psychiatric report; ensure the condition is a recognised medical condition; advise on plea and sentence implications.
legal_reference: Homicide Act 1957 s.2 (as amended by Coroners and Justice Act 2009); IPC s.84 (insanity)

name: Drug Offences — Possession and Supply
consequence: Possession of a controlled drug is a criminal offence; supply carries substantially higher penalties. In India, the NDPS Act 1985 provides rigorous imprisonment and mandatory minimum sentences for commercial quantities.
recommended_action: Classify the drug (Class A/B/C in UK; Schedule I/II under NDPS in India); assess quantity for commercial/personal use distinction; advise on bail restrictions under NDPS s.37.
legal_reference: Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 (UK); Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act 1985 (India)

name: Bribery and Corruption
consequence: Bribery of a public official or in a commercial context is a serious criminal offence. In India, Prevention of Corruption Act 1988 applies to public servants with Lokpal oversight. UK Bribery Act 2010 has strict corporate liability.
recommended_action: Companies should implement adequate procedures under Bribery Act 2010 s.7; in India file complaint with CBI/Anti-Corruption Bureau; preserve documentary evidence.
legal_reference: Bribery Act 2010 (UK); Prevention of Corruption Act 1988 (India); UNCAC

name: Cybercrime — Unauthorised Access
consequence: Unauthorised access to computer systems is a criminal offence. In India, IT Act 2000 ss.43, 66 apply. UK Computer Misuse Act 1990 provides for up to 10 years for serious cases.
recommended_action: Preserve digital forensic evidence; report to police cyber cell; in India report to CERT-In; consider parallel civil claim for breach of confidence.
legal_reference: Computer Misuse Act 1990 (UK); Information Technology Act 2000 ss.43, 66, 66C (India)

name: Fundamental Rights — Article 19/21 (India)
consequence: Article 21 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the right to life and personal liberty. Article 19 guarantees six freedoms. These are enforceable against the State. Article 32/226 provides constitutional remedies.
recommended_action: File writ petition under Art.32 (Supreme Court) or Art.226 (High Court); identify State action; assess whether restriction satisfies reasonable restriction criteria under Art.19(2)-(6).
legal_reference: Constitution of India Arts.12-35; Maneka Gandhi v Union of India [1978] 1 SCC 248; Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala [1973]

name: Judicial Review — Ultra Vires
consequence: In UK, judicial review is available on grounds of illegality, irrationality (Wednesbury unreasonableness), or procedural impropriety. In India, writ of certiorari, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and habeas corpus are available.
recommended_action: Apply for permission to apply for judicial review within 3 months of decision (UK); in India file writ petition within reasonable time; identify the relevant ground.
legal_reference: Senior Courts Act 1981 s.31 (UK); Constitution of India Arts.32 and 226; Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister [1985] AC 374

name: Legitimate Expectation
consequence: A public authority that makes a clear and unambiguous representation to an individual may not frustrate the resulting legitimate expectation without good reason. Substantive legitimate expectations may be protected by the court.
recommended_action: Document the representation made by the public authority; establish reliance; advise whether the authority has good reason to resile from the representation.
legal_reference: R v North and East Devon HA ex parte Coughlan [2001] QB 213; Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister [1985]

name: Human Rights Act — Convention Rights
consequence: Public authorities must act compatibly with ECHR Convention rights. Key rights: Art.6 (fair trial), Art.8 (privacy), Art.10 (expression), Art.14 (non-discrimination). Incompatibility with HRA triggers declaration.
recommended_action: Identify the Convention right engaged; assess whether any interference is lawful, necessary, and proportionate; consider HRA s.4 declaration of incompatibility.
legal_reference: Human Rights Act 1998; European Convention on Human Rights; R (Daly) v Secretary of State [2001] UKHL 26

name: Equality Before Law — Article 14 (India)
consequence: Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. A law or executive action will survive challenge if it makes an intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to the object sought to be achieved.
recommended_action: Challenge arbitrary State action through writ petition; establish that the classification fails the intelligible differentia/rational nexus test; seek mandamus or declaration.
legal_reference: Constitution of India Art.14; E.P. Royappa v State of Tamil Nadu [1974] 4 SCC 3; Maneka Gandhi v Union of India [1978]

name: Divorce — Grounds and Process
consequence: In UK, no-fault divorce is available after a 20-week reflection period under Divorce, Dissolution and Separation Act 2020. In India, Hindu Marriage Act 1955 provides grounds including adultery, cruelty, desertion, and mutual consent.
recommended_action: Advise on the appropriate ground; consider mediation; address financial remedies; advise on impact on children arrangements; in India assess applicable personal law.
legal_reference: Divorce, Dissolution and Separation Act 2020 (UK); Hindu Marriage Act 1955 ss.13-13B (India); Special Marriage Act 1954 (India)

name: Child Custody and Welfare
consequence: The paramount consideration in all child matters is the welfare of the child. Courts apply a welfare checklist. In India, the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 and Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act 1956 apply.
recommended_action: Prepare evidence of the child's welfare; engage a CAFCASS officer (UK); in India apply to Family Court under Guardians and Wards Act 1890; consider mediation to minimise harm.
legal_reference: Children Act 1989 s.1 (UK); Guardians and Wards Act 1890 (India); Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act 1956 (India)

name: Domestic Violence — Non-Molestation and Occupation Orders
consequence: A non-molestation order prohibits molestation; breach is a criminal offence. An occupation order regulates who lives in the family home. In India, Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 provides civil remedies.
recommended_action: Apply for without-notice non-molestation order in urgent cases; in India approach Protection Officer or Magistrate under PWDVA 2005; advise on criminal complaint for IPC s.498A (cruelty by husband).
legal_reference: Family Law Act 1996 ss.42-63 (UK); Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 (India); IPC s.498A

name: Financial Remedies on Divorce
consequence: On divorce, courts have wide discretion to make financial orders including lump sums, property adjustment, and periodical payments. The starting point for long marriages is equal division. In India, maintenance is under CrPC s.125 and Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act.
recommended_action: Prepare Form E financial statement; consider clean break; advise on pension sharing; in India advise on maintenance application under CrPC s.125 or HMA s.25.
legal_reference: Matrimonial Causes Act 1973 ss.23-25 (UK); Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act 1956; CrPC s.125 (India)

name: Prenuptial Agreements
consequence: Prenuptial agreements are not automatically binding in UK but will be given decisive weight if Radmacher criteria are met (freely entered, understanding, not unfair). In India prenups have limited enforceability.
recommended_action: Advise both parties to have independent legal advice; ensure no undue pressure; disclose all assets; enter at least 28 days before wedding; include review clause.
legal_reference: Radmacher v Granatino [2010] UKSC 42; Matrimonial Causes Act 1973 s.25

name: Directors' Duties — Section 172 Duty to Promote Success
consequence: A director must act in the way they consider, in good faith, would be most likely to promote the success of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole, having regard to long-term consequences, employees, suppliers, community, and environment.
recommended_action: Directors should document decision-making process considering all s.172 factors; board minutes should reflect deliberation; independent legal advice recommended for complex transactions.
legal_reference: Companies Act 2006 s.172 (UK); Companies Act 2013 ss.149, 166 (India)

name: Directors — Conflict of Interest
consequence: A director must avoid situations where they have, or could have, an interest that conflicts or may conflict with the interests of the company. Authorisation by independent directors or shareholders is required.
recommended_action: Disclose conflict to the board; obtain shareholder or independent director authorisation; document the disclosure and authorisation in board minutes.
legal_reference: Companies Act 2006 ss.175-177 (UK); Companies Act 2013 ss.184-188 (India)

name: Unfair Prejudice — Shareholder Remedy
consequence: A shareholder may petition for relief where the company's affairs are being conducted in a manner unfairly prejudicial to their interests. In India, NCLT has jurisdiction under Companies Act 2013 s.241-242 for oppression and mismanagement.
recommended_action: Gather evidence of prejudicial conduct; consider whether exit route or buy-out order is sought; in India file application to NCLT under s.241; act within limitation.
legal_reference: Companies Act 2006 s.994 (UK); Companies Act 2013 ss.241-244 (India); O'Neill v Phillips [1999] 1 WLR 1092

name: Wrongful Trading
consequence: A director may be liable to contribute to a company's assets if they continued to trade when they knew or ought to have known there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation, and failed to take every step to minimise losses.
recommended_action: Advise directors to cease trading immediately if insolvent; take independent legal advice; convene board meeting; consider voluntary liquidation; document all decisions.
legal_reference: Insolvency Act 1986 s.214 (UK); Companies Act 2013 s.339 (India)

name: Piercing the Corporate Veil
consequence: The corporate veil will only be pierced in very limited circumstances: where it is a deliberate abuse of the corporate form to evade an existing legal obligation, or where statute so requires.
recommended_action: Assess whether the Prest v Petrodel criteria are met; gather evidence of deliberate evasion; consider equitable remedies over veil piercing; in India courts are equally reluctant.
legal_reference: Salomon v Salomon [1897] AC 22; Prest v Petrodel Resources [2013] UKSC 34; Tata Engineering v State of Bihar [1965] SC

name: Insolvency — Administration
consequence: Administration imposes an automatic moratorium on legal proceedings. The administrator's primary purpose is to rescue the company as a going concern. Pre-pack administrations must comply with SIP 16 and the Administration (Restrictions on Disposal) Rules.
recommended_action: Appoint qualified insolvency practitioner; consider pre-pack viability; ensure SIP 16 compliance for pre-packs; notify creditors within 28 days; advise on CIGA 2020 moratorium as alternative.
legal_reference: Insolvency Act 1986 Schedule B1; Corporate Insolvency and Governance Act 2020; Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016 (India)

name: IBC — Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (India)
consequence: Under IBC 2016, a financial creditor or operational creditor may trigger CIRP at NCLT for default of ₹1 crore or more. The CIRP must be completed within 330 days. The resolution plan must meet minimum thresholds for creditors.
recommended_action: File application at NCLT with evidence of default; IRP is appointed to manage affairs; Committee of Creditors formed; invite resolution plans; if no plan approved, proceed to liquidation.
legal_reference: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016 ss.7-9; IBC Regulations 2016; Swiss Ribbons v Union of India [2019] SC

name: UK GDPR / Data Protection — Lawful Basis
consequence: Processing personal data is lawful only if a lawful basis under UK GDPR Art.6 applies. Consent must be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous. Legitimate interests must not override the data subject's rights.
recommended_action: Document the lawful basis for each processing activity in the ROPA; review consent mechanisms for bundling or pre-ticked boxes; conduct LIA for legitimate interests processing.
legal_reference: UK GDPR Art.6; Data Protection Act 2018; Information Technology (Amendment) Act 2008 and DPDP Act 2023 (India)

name: Data Breach — Notification Obligation
consequence: A personal data breach that poses a risk to individuals must be notified to the ICO within 72 hours. High-risk breaches must also be notified to affected individuals. In India, CERT-In requires breach reporting within 6 hours.
recommended_action: Activate incident response plan immediately; assess risk threshold; notify ICO within 72 hours if risk threshold met; preserve forensic evidence; notify affected individuals if high risk.
legal_reference: UK GDPR Arts. 33-34; CERT-In Directions 2022 (India); Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 (India)

name: Data Subject Rights — Access and Erasure
consequence: Data subjects have the right to access their personal data within one month of a DSAR. The right to erasure applies where data is no longer necessary, consent is withdrawn, or processing is unlawful.
recommended_action: Respond to DSAR within one calendar month (extendable to 3 months for complex requests); assess erasure grounds; advise on exemptions (legal claims, public interest); document all decisions.
legal_reference: UK GDPR Arts.15-17; DPDP Act 2023 ss.11-12 (India)

name: International Data Transfers
consequence: Transfer of personal data outside the UK requires an appropriate safeguard such as an adequacy decision, UK SCCs, BCRs, or derogation. Transfers to India may rely on emerging adequacy or SCCs.
recommended_action: Assess the transfer mechanism; execute UK International Data Transfer Agreement (IDTA) or UK SCCs; conduct Transfer Impact Assessment for high-risk destinations.
legal_reference: UK GDPR Arts.44-49; Information Commissioner's Office Transfer Guidance 2022

name: Consumer Rights — Goods: Satisfactory Quality
consequence: Goods must be of satisfactory quality, fit for purpose, and as described. In the first 30 days, the consumer has the right to reject. After 30 days, the right to repair or replace arises. In India, Consumer Protection Act 2019 applies.
recommended_action: Advise consumer on the appropriate remedy stage; document defect; for rejection within 30 days demand refund; report to Consumer Forum under Consumer Protection Act 2019 (India).
legal_reference: Consumer Rights Act 2015 ss.9-24 (UK); Consumer Protection Act 2019 (India)

name: Unfair Contract Terms — Consumer
consequence: A term in a consumer contract is unfair and unenforceable if it causes a significant imbalance in the parties' rights and obligations to the detriment of the consumer, contrary to good faith.
recommended_action: Assess the term against the grey list of suspect terms; advise consumer the term is not binding; core terms (price and subject matter) are exempt if transparent and prominent.
legal_reference: Consumer Rights Act 2015 ss.62-68 (UK); Consumer Protection Act 2019 s.2(47) (India)

name: Abuse of Dominant Position
consequence: It is unlawful for a dominant undertaking to abuse its position. Abuse includes predatory pricing, excessive pricing, refusal to supply, tying, and exclusivity arrangements. In India, CCI enforces Competition Act 2002.
recommended_action: Define the relevant market; assess dominance (>30% indicative in India, 40%+ in UK); gather evidence of abusive conduct; file complaint with CMA (UK) or CCI (India).
legal_reference: Competition Act 1998 s.18 (UK); Competition Act 2002 ss.4, 19 (India); TFEU Art.102

name: Anti-Competitive Agreements — Cartel
consequence: Agreements between competitors that fix prices, share markets, or rig bids are object restrictions — automatically infringes competition law with no need to prove effects. Individuals can be imprisoned for cartel offences.
recommended_action: Consider leniency application to CMA/CCI immediately; preserve all communications; advise on criminal exposure for individuals; assess scope of damages claims.
legal_reference: Competition Act 1998 s.2 (UK); Competition Act 2002 s.3 (India); Enterprise Act 2002 s.188 (criminal cartel)

name: Arbitration Agreement — Validity and Scope
consequence: An arbitration agreement must be in writing. It is separable from the main contract (separability doctrine). Courts will stay proceedings and refer parties to arbitration if there is a valid arbitration agreement covering the dispute.
recommended_action: Check the scope of the arbitration clause; assert kompetenz-kompetenz (tribunal rules on its own jurisdiction); apply for stay of court proceedings under Arbitration Act s.9 / Arbitration and Conciliation Act s.8 (India).
legal_reference: Arbitration Act 1996 ss.7-9 (UK); Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 ss.7-8 (India); UNCITRAL Model Law

name: Enforcement of Arbitral Awards
consequence: A foreign arbitral award from a New York Convention state is enforceable in India/UK as a decree of the court. Grounds for refusal are limited: invalid arbitration agreement, no proper notice, award outside scope, public policy.
recommended_action: Apply to enforce award under Arbitration Act s.101 (UK) or Arbitration and Conciliation Act s.44-48 (India); narrow grounds for challenge; public policy objection is construed narrowly.
legal_reference: New York Convention 1958; Arbitration Act 1996 s.101 (UK); Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 s.48 (India)

name: Legal Professional Privilege
consequence: Legal advice privilege protects confidential communications between lawyer and client for the purpose of giving legal advice. Litigation privilege covers all communications when litigation is reasonably contemplated. LPP is an absolute right.
recommended_action: Review communications to confirm they satisfy LPP requirements (dominant purpose for litigation privilege); assert privilege in disclosure; LPP cannot be waived inadvertently without careful review.
legal_reference: Three Rivers DC v Bank of England (No.6) [2004] UKHL 48; R (Morgan Grenfell) v Special Commissioner [2003] 1 AC 563

name: Without Prejudice Rule
trigger_keywords: without prejudice save as to costs
consequence: Communications made in a genuine attempt to settle a dispute are inadmissible in evidence as without prejudice, even if not expressly marked. WPSATC is admissible on costs after judgment.
recommended_action: Mark all settlement correspondence 'Without Prejudice'; advise that the label is not conclusive; WPSATC creates a separate admissibility regime for the costs stage.
legal_reference: Rush & Tompkins v GLC [1989] AC 1280; Oceanbulk Shipping v TMT Asia [2010] UKSC 44

name: Hearsay Evidence
consequence: Hearsay evidence is admissible in civil proceedings subject to notice requirements. In criminal proceedings, hearsay is admissible only where a statutory or preserved common law gateway applies (CJA 2003).
recommended_action: In civil cases serve CJA 1995 notice of intention to rely on hearsay; in criminal cases identify the applicable gateway; assess weight and reliability concerns.
legal_reference: Civil Evidence Act 1995; Criminal Justice Act 2003 ss.114-136; Indian Evidence Act 1872 ss.60-65

name: Mortgages — Right to Possession and Repossession
consequence: A mortgagee has the right to possession of residential property in default, but the court may adjourn possession proceedings if the mortgagor is likely to pay off arrears within a reasonable time.
recommended_action: Advise mortgagor to contact lender immediately; apply for suspended possession order; check compliance with Pre-Action Protocol for Mortgage Repossession; in India see SARFAESI Act 2002.
legal_reference: Administration of Justice Act 1970 s.36; Cheltenham & Gloucester BS v Norgan [1996] 1 WLR 343; SARFAESI Act 2002 (India)

name: Restrictive Covenants — Benefit and Burden
consequence: The burden of a restrictive covenant runs with freehold land in equity if it is negative, touches and concerns the land, there is a dominant tenement, and it was intended to run. The benefit runs at law or equity.
recommended_action: Check Land Register for registered covenants; advise developer on covenant modification application to Upper Tribunal (Lands Chamber) under LPA 1925 s.84; consider insurance.
legal_reference: Tulk v Moxhay [1848] 2 Ph 774; Law of Property Act 1925 s.84; Transfer of Property Act 1882 (India)

name: Limitation Period — General Contract
consequence: A simple contract claim becomes time-barred six years from the date of breach (UK) or three years from when the right to sue accrues (India). Specialty contracts attract 12 years in UK.
recommended_action: Calculate breach date and remaining limitation window; advise on issuing protective claim before expiry; in India check if s.14 or s.17 Limitation Act 1963 exceptions apply.
legal_reference: Limitation Act 1980 s.5 (UK); Limitation Act 1963 (India)

name: Force Majeure Clause
consequence: Force majeure clauses are construed strictly; frustration may discharge the contract only if performance is radically different. ICA s.56 codifies the frustration doctrine in India.
recommended_action: Review clause wording for notification obligations and scope; assess whether the event prevents (not merely hinders) performance; give notice within the prescribed time.
legal_reference: Davis Contractors v Fareham UDC [1956] AC 696; Indian Contract Act 1872 s.56; Energy Charter Treaty cases

name: Natural Justice — Right to a Fair Hearing
consequence: Natural justice requires: (1) the right to be heard (audi alteram partem) — adequate notice and opportunity to respond; (2) rule against bias (nemo judex in sua causa). Breach renders a decision voidable.
recommended_action: Advise the affected party to object at the earliest opportunity; apply for judicial review or appeal as appropriate; establish that the breach caused actual prejudice.
legal_reference: Ridge v Baldwin [1964] AC 40; R v Secretary of State ex parte Doody [1994] 1 AC 531; A.K. Kraipak v Union of India [1970] SC

name: Rule Against Bias — Apparent Bias
consequence: A decision maker must not have a personal interest in the outcome or a real possibility of bias. The test for apparent bias is whether a fair-minded and informed observer would conclude there was a real possibility of bias.
recommended_action: Apply for recusal at the earliest opportunity; if bias materialises, seek appeal or judicial review; automatic disqualification applies for pecuniary interest.
legal_reference: Porter v Magill [2002] 2 AC 357; Dimes v Proprietors of Grand Junction Canal [1852]; Ranjit Thakur v Union of India [1987] SC

name: Asylum — Well-Founded Fear of Persecution
consequence: A refugee is a person outside their country of nationality with a well-founded fear of persecution on grounds of race, religion, nationality, political opinion, or membership of a particular social group. Non-refoulement principle prohibits return to a country of persecution.
recommended_action: Gather country of origin information; submit asylum claim promptly; prepare detailed witness statement; attend asylum interview with legal representative; challenge removal if non-refoulement risk.
legal_reference: Refugee Convention 1951 Art.1A(2); Human Rights Act 1998 Art.3; Nationality and Borders Act 2022 (UK)

name: Tax Evasion vs Tax Avoidance
consequence: Tax evasion (illegal) involves deliberately misrepresenting or concealing information. Tax avoidance uses legal means but aggressive schemes may be caught by GAAR. GAAR applies to arrangements whose main benefit is a tax advantage in abusive arrangements.
recommended_action: Assess whether the arrangement is caught by GAAR; advise on DOTAS disclosure obligations; in India assess GAAR under IT Act ss.95-102; consider voluntary disclosure.
legal_reference: Finance Act 2013 ss.206-215 (UK GAAR); Income Tax Act 1961 ss.95-102 (India GAAR); Criminal Finances Act 2017

name: Transfer Pricing
consequence: Transactions between related parties must be priced at arm's length. Tax authorities may adjust the price of related-party transactions to reflect arm's length values. India has mandatory APA and safe harbour rules.
recommended_action: Document the arm's length analysis for all related-party transactions; prepare contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation; consider APA to obtain certainty on methodology.
legal_reference: OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines; Income Tax Act 1961 ss.92-92F (India); TIOPA 2010 Part 4 (UK)

name: Environmental Permit — Enforcement
consequence: Operating without an environmental permit or in breach of permit conditions is a criminal offence. The Environment Agency (UK) or CPCB (India) can serve enforcement notices, stop notices, and prosecute for unlimited fines.
recommended_action: Secure or review environmental permits; conduct environmental audit; respond promptly to enforcement notices; consider voluntary remediation to mitigate penalties.
legal_reference: Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016; Water Act 1981 (India); Environment (Protection) Act 1986 (India)

name: Medical Negligence — Bolam/Bolitho Standard
consequence: A doctor is not negligent if they acted in accordance with a responsible body of medical opinion (Bolam). However, the court may reject that body of opinion if it is not logically defensible (Bolitho). In India, the Jacob Mathew test applies.
recommended_action: Commission independent medical expert evidence; obtain full medical records; assess causation between breach and harm; consider CNO claim in UK or consumer forum/civil court in India.
legal_reference: Bolam v Friern Hospital Management Committee [1957] 1 WLR 582; Bolitho v City and Hackney HA [1998] AC 232; Jacob Mathew v State of Punjab [2005] SC

name: Financial Services — Regulated Activities
consequence: Carrying on regulated financial activities without FCA authorisation is a criminal offence (s.23 FSMA 2000) and contracts made in breach are unenforceable. In India, SEBI regulates securities markets and RBI regulates banking.
recommended_action: Verify FCA/SEBI authorisation before engaging in regulated activities; check financial promotions are approved by an authorised person; apply for appropriate regulatory permissions.
legal_reference: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 ss.19-26 (UK); SEBI Act 1992; RBI Act 1934 (India)

name: Anti-Money Laundering — SAR Obligations
consequence: Regulated entities must file Suspicious Activity Reports where they know or suspect money laundering. Tipping off the subject of a SAR is a criminal offence. In India, PMLA 2002 requires reporting entities to file STRs with FIU-IND.
recommended_action: File SAR/STR with NCA (UK) or FIU-IND (India) immediately; do not tip off; obtain consent before proceeding with transaction; freeze proceeds pending SAR outcome.
legal_reference: Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 ss.327-340 (UK); Prevention of Money Laundering Act 2002 (India); Money Laundering Regulations 2017 (UK)

name: RERA — Real Estate Regulation (India)
consequence: RERA 2016 mandates developer registration, escrow of 70% of funds, disclosure of project details, and timely delivery. A buyer can claim interest at SBI MCLR + 2% on delay; repeated default may lead to registration cancellation.
recommended_action: File complaint with State RERA Authority; seek interest for delay and refund if possession not delivered; developers must complete the project before offering possession.
legal_reference: Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act 2016 (India); State RERA Rules

name: Stamp Duty and Registration
consequence: An unregistered document relating to immovable property of value exceeding ₹100 (India) cannot be used as evidence (Registration Act 1908 s.49). In UK, SDLT must be paid within 14 days of completion.
recommended_action: Ensure proper stamping and registration before relying on property documents; in UK file SDLT return within 14 days; advise on penalties for late SDLT or Indian stamp duty deficiency.
legal_reference: Registration Act 1908 (India); Indian Stamp Act 1899; Stamp Duty Land Tax Act 2003 (UK)

name: Consumer Forum — Deficiency in Service
consequence: A consumer can file a complaint for deficiency in services or unfair trade practices before District/State/National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (DCDRC/SCDRC/NCDRC) depending on the claim value. Compensation, replacement, and refund can be ordered.
recommended_action: Calculate claim value to determine appropriate forum; file complaint within 2 years of cause of action (extendable for sufficient cause); preserve all evidence, bills, and correspondence.
legal_reference: Consumer Protection Act 2019 ss.34-58 (India)

name: Right to Information — India
consequence: Any citizen can request information from public authorities under RTI Act 2005. The PIO must respond within 30 days (48 hours for life/liberty matters). Failure attracts penalty of ₹250/day up to ₹25,000.
recommended_action: File RTI application to the PIO of the relevant public authority; if denied or unsatisfied, appeal to First Appellate Authority within 30 days; second appeal to Central/State Information Commission.
legal_reference: Right to Information Act 2005 (India)

name: IT Act — Section 66A Struck Down
consequence: Section 66A of the IT Act 2000, which penalised 'offensive' online messages, was struck down as unconstitutional (Shreya Singhal v Union of India [2015]). Any prosecution under s.66A is void.
recommended_action: Challenge any prosecution brought under s.66A as unconstitutional; advise police that the provision is void; refer to Shreya Singhal judgment.
legal_reference: Shreya Singhal v Union of India [2015] AIR SC 1523; Information Technology Act 2000 s.66A (struck down)

name: Intestate Succession — Hindu Law
consequence: On intestacy of a male Hindu, Class I heirs (widow, sons, daughters, mother) take equal shares. Daughters have equal coparcenary rights since the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005. For Muslims, personal law applies.
recommended_action: Identify the applicable personal law; prepare Schedule of Class I/II heirs; obtain succession certificate from Civil Court; probate required for immovable property above threshold.
legal_reference: Hindu Succession Act 1956 ss.8-13 (as amended 2005); Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937; Indian Succession Act 1925

name: Wills — Validity and Probate
consequence: A valid will requires testamentary capacity, knowledge and approval, no undue influence, proper execution (signed by testator in presence of two witnesses who also sign). In India, attestation by two witnesses is mandatory under Indian Succession Act 1925.
recommended_action: Ensure will is properly executed and attested; advise on probate application; assess testamentary capacity if challenged; consider statutory wills for incapacitated persons.
legal_reference: Wills Act 1837 (UK); Indian Succession Act 1925 ss.59-63; Administration of Estates Act 1925 (UK)

name: Motor Vehicle Accident — Third Party Liability
consequence: In India, third party motor insurance is mandatory under Motor Vehicles Act 1988. Victims can file compensation claims before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal (MACT). Structured formula applies for fatal accidents.
recommended_action: File FIR immediately; obtain accident report; file MACT claim within limitation; gather evidence of income and dependency for fatal accident claims; insurer is vicariously liable.
legal_reference: Motor Vehicles Act 1988 ss.140-168 (India); Road Traffic Act 1988 (UK)

name: Strike and Lockout — India
consequence: Workers in public utility services must give 14-day notice before striking. Strikes without notice or during conciliation proceedings are illegal under the Industrial Disputes Act 1947. Participation in illegal strikes may justify dismissal.
recommended_action: Verify whether advance notice was given; assess whether the strike is in a public utility service; advise employer on lawful lockout procedure; refer dispute to conciliation officer.
legal_reference: Industrial Disputes Act 1947 ss.22-26 (India)

name: Habeas Corpus
consequence: A writ of habeas corpus requires a person detained to be brought before the court to determine the legality of detention. In India it is available under Art.32 (SC) and Art.226 (HC). Preventive detention laws are subject to procedural safeguards under Art.22.
recommended_action: File habeas corpus petition immediately; advise on grounds — detention without legal authority, breach of Art.22 safeguards; in UK apply to Divisional Court; Administrative Court acts urgently.
legal_reference: Constitution of India Arts.22, 32, 226; Habeas Corpus Act 1679 (UK); ADM Jabalpur v Shiv Kant Shukla [1976] (overruled by Puttaswamy)

name: Right to Privacy — India (Puttaswamy)
consequence: The right to privacy is a fundamental right under Art.21 of the Indian Constitution (K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India [2017]). State intrusion must be legal, necessary, and proportionate. The DPDP Act 2023 provides statutory privacy framework.
recommended_action: Challenge State intrusion on privacy through writ petition under Art.32/226; assess necessity and proportionality; advise on DPDP Act 2023 rights including consent withdrawal.
legal_reference: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India [2017] 10 SCC 1; Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 (India)

name: Limitation — India (Limitation Act 1963)
consequence: Different limitation periods apply to different causes of action under the Limitation Act 1963. Courts may condone delay under s.5 for appeals if sufficient cause is shown. The limitation period for suits is generally 3 years.
recommended_action: Check the applicable article in the Limitation Act 1963 Schedule; file within limitation; if delayed, prepare application for condonation of delay under s.5 with affidavit showing sufficient cause.
legal_reference: Limitation Act 1963 (India); Collector Land Acquisition v Mst Katiji [1987] SC

name: Injunctions — Interim Relief
consequence: An interim injunction is granted where: there is a serious question to be tried, the balance of convenience favours the injunction, and damages would not be an adequate remedy (American Cyanamid). In India, the test is prima facie case, balance of convenience, and irreparable harm.
recommended_action: Move urgently for ex parte injunction if necessary; cross-undertaking in damages required; serve with notice; in India file IA under CPC Order XXXIX Rules 1-2.
legal_reference: American Cyanamid v Ethicon [1975] AC 396; CPC 1908 Order XXXIX (India); Senior Courts Act 1981 s.37 (UK)
